name: Subject-verb agreement basics (singular vs plural)
scope: The foundation rule the whole strand rests on. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION punchline -- 'The dog RUN across the yard' vs the correct 'The dog RUNS across the yard'; a singular subject takes a singular verb (the -s at the end of the VERB, oddly, marks it as singular in the present tense). T2: the mirror case -- 'The dogs RUNS across the yard' vs the correct 'The dogs RUN'; a plural subject takes a plural verb (no -s on the verb). T3: naming the categories in-context -- given a real quoted sentence, identify which word is the SUBJECT (the noun doing the action) and which is the VERB (the action word), and check whether they agree in number. T4: the intervening-phrase trap -- 'The BOX of chocolates ARE on the table' vs correct 'The BOX of chocolates IS on the table'; a prepositional phrase between subject and verb does NOT change the subject (box is singular; 'of chocolates' is a modifier). T5: multi-clause verdict -- given a paragraph, identify every subject-verb pair and flag the one that disagrees, distinguishing an agreement error from a tense error.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'agreement, subject-verb'; Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.138-5.145. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Subject-verb agreement' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the general rule and the intervening-phrase trap examples. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify the -s-on-the-verb-marks-singular framing in Merriam-Webster before writing T1.
framing_note: Punchline via misuse: the WRONG sentence is quoted in the stem and sounds obviously off ('The dog run across the yard' -- a kid hears it). Vocab-teaching invariant at T3: define SUBJECT and VERB inline with the example. Everyday apolitical scenes only -- pets, homework, family, sports. Distractor pool: tense errors ('had ran' vs 'had run'), pronoun-case errors ('me and my brother went'), homophone errors ('their/there'). CHOICE PARITY: if answer is a corrected sentence, all four choices are similar-length corrected/miscorrected sentences.

name: Collective nouns: team, family, jury (US vs UK)
scope: The collective-noun agreement judgment. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION punchline for American English -- 'The team ARE winning' sounds odd to American ears; the standard American form is 'The team IS winning' (the team acts as one unit). T2: define COLLECTIVE NOUN in-context -- a word for a group treated as a single thing (team, family, jury, committee, class, band, crowd, audience, staff). T3: the British-English exception -- BBC football commentary regularly says 'Manchester United ARE playing well tonight' because British English treats collective nouns as plural when the members act individually; both forms are correct in their register. T4: the emphasis-shifts-the-verb case -- 'The jury IS deliberating' (acting as one body) vs 'The jury ARE arguing among themselves' (individual members disagreeing); the sentence's MEANING controls the verb. T5: the tricky mixed case -- 'The couple IS/ARE celebrating their anniversary' (their is plural, so 'the couple ARE' is more consistent; but 'The couple IS registered at the hotel' treats them as a single unit). Identify which form fits the intent.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.7 (collective nouns); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'collective nouns'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Collective noun' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the US vs UK convention split and the BBC football-commentary example.
framing_note: Punchline via misuse + register contrast. Vocab-teaching invariant: T2 defines 'collective noun' inline. Apolitical safe examples: sports teams, juries, families, orchestras -- no political parties or activist groups. Distractor pool: other agreement traps (indefinite pronouns, compound subjects), other verb errors. CHOICE PARITY across corrected sentences.

name: Compound subjects with AND: usually plural, sometimes singular
scope: The compound-subject-with-AND rule and its exception. T1: the canonical case -- 'Peanut butter and jelly ARE spread on the bread' -- two things joined by AND normally take a plural verb. T2: the mirror wrong-version -- 'My brother and my sister IS coming over' sounds off; correct is 'My brother and my sister ARE coming over'. T3: the CONCEPTUAL-SINGLE exception -- 'Peanut butter and jelly IS my favorite sandwich' takes SINGULAR because the two items name ONE thing (a single sandwich). Another example: 'Bread and butter IS what I want for breakfast'. T4: identify which is which -- given four compound-and sentences, pick the one where the compound names a single conceptual thing and correctly uses IS. T5: the borderline judgment -- 'Macaroni and cheese IS/ARE on the menu' (one dish, singular preferred); 'The salt and pepper ARE on the table' (two separate shakers, plural preferred). Meaning drives the verb.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.140; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'compound subjects'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Subject-verb agreement' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the peanut-butter-and-jelly and bread-and-butter conceptual-single examples.
framing_note: Punchline via the tasty conceptual-single flip. Everyday food scenes (sandwiches, breakfast, dinner) -- no political examples. Distractor pool: other compound-subject rules (OR/NOR nearer-subject), collective noun errors, indefinite pronoun errors.

name: Compound subjects with OR/NOR: the nearer-subject rule
scope: The one agreement rule most adults get wrong. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Neither the coach nor the players IS ready' sounds off; correct is 'Neither the coach nor the players ARE ready' -- the verb agrees with the NEARER subject (players, plural). T2: flip the subject order and the verb changes -- 'Neither the players nor the coach IS ready' becomes correct with IS (coach, singular, is nearer). T3: same rule with EITHER/OR -- 'Either the cat or the dogs are outside' vs 'Either the dogs or the cat is outside' -- the noun closest to the verb wins. T4: the writer's escape hatch -- if the mismatched pair sounds awkward either way, REORDER the subjects to put the plural nearer the verb ('Neither the coach nor the players are ready' reads more smoothly than the reverse). T5: the compound-with-nor across mixed persons -- 'Neither he nor I AM going' vs 'Neither I nor he IS going'; agreement is with both number AND person of the nearer subject, though most writers rewrite these to avoid the mouthful.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.141 (either-or, neither-nor); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'either'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Subject-verb agreement' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the nearer-subject rule.
framing_note: Punchline via the order-flip -- the same two nouns, different verb, depending on which comes closer. Apolitical examples (coaches, players, pets). Distractor pool: AND compound rules (all-plural), collective nouns, indefinite pronouns.

name: Indefinite pronouns: everyone, each, either take singular verbs
scope: The always-singular indefinite-pronoun list. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Everyone ARE bringing a dish' sounds off; correct is 'Everyone IS bringing a dish'. Despite meaning many people, EVERYONE is grammatically singular. T2: define INDEFINITE PRONOUN in-context and quote the always-singular list -- everyone, everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, no one, nobody, each, either, neither. T3: the trap of the plural-sounding modifier -- 'Each of the students HAS a book' (not HAVE); 'Everyone in the seats WAS cheering' (not WERE) -- the intervening prepositional phrase does not change the singular pronoun. T4: the plural-always cases for contrast -- BOTH, FEW, MANY, SEVERAL are always plural ('Both are ready', 'Several were missing'). T5: the depends-on-referent cases -- SOME, ANY, ALL, NONE, MOST can be singular OR plural depending on what they refer to ('Some of the water IS gone' vs 'Some of the students ARE gone'); mass noun = singular, count noun = plural.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.68-5.70 (indefinite pronouns); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'agreement: indefinite pronouns'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Indefinite pronoun' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the singular/plural/either lists.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching invariant: T2 defines 'indefinite pronoun' inline with the full list. Punchline via the natural mis-hearing ('everyone ARE' feels right and is wrong). Everyday examples (potluck, classroom, playground). Distractor pool: collective nouns, compound subjects.

name: Measurements and amounts: 'Two hundred miles IS a long drive'
scope: The plural-looking-but-singular subject rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Two hundred miles ARE a long drive' sounds off; correct is 'Two hundred miles IS a long drive'. When an amount is treated as a single quantity, it takes a SINGULAR verb, even though it looks plural. T2: money -- 'Ten dollars IS the price' (not ARE); the amount is one price. T3: time -- 'Three hours IS enough time' (not ARE); the amount is one duration. Distances, weights, volumes work the same way: 'Five pounds IS heavy', 'Two gallons IS all we have'. T4: the exception -- when the plural nouns are being counted individually rather than named as a total, the verb goes plural: 'Ten dollar bills WERE scattered on the floor' (ten separate bills, plural) vs 'Ten dollars IS on the table' (one amount, singular). T5: the borderline judgment -- 'The three years I spent in college WERE the best of my life' (the years are counted individually as experiences) vs 'Three years IS a long time to wait' (the amount as a single span); intent controls the verb.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.142 (nouns of measurement); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'agreement, subject-verb: quantity'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Subject-verb agreement' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the amount-as-single-unit rule.
framing_note: Punchline via the counterintuitive singular ('Two hundred miles IS' feels wrong until you hear the logic). Apolitical examples (drives, prices, homework time, cooking amounts). Distractor pool: collective nouns, indefinite pronouns.

name: Titles of works: 'The New York Times IS a newspaper'
scope: The title-as-singular-thing rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'The New York Times ARE reporting the story' sounds off; correct is 'The New York Times IS reporting the story'. A title -- even one that ends in an -s or names plural things -- is ONE work, and takes a singular verb. T2: 'Star Wars IS a movie' (not ARE, though 'wars' is plural); 'The Chronicles of Narnia IS a book series'. T3: works with plural-sounding titles -- 'Little Women IS a novel by Louisa May Alcott' (published 1868); 'Great Expectations IS a Dickens novel' (1861). The words inside the title don't determine the verb; the title as a WHOLE does. T4: bands and musical groups follow the American convention as singular units -- 'The Beatles IS a band from Liverpool' (American style); British commentary would say 'The Beatles ARE'. Both forms are heard in the wild. T5: species and Latin-plural titles -- 'Mathematics IS my favorite subject' (looks plural, is singular); 'Politics IS a rough business'; 'The news IS on at six' (news looks plural, always singular). These -ics words and news are conventionally singular in modern usage.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 8.163 (titles as singular); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entries 'mathematics' and 'news'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Grammatical number' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the -ics-as-singular convention and titles-as-singular convention.
framing_note: Punchline via the plural-looking title paired with a singular verb. Real works cited (Little Women 1868, Great Expectations 1861, The New York Times, Star Wars) as neutral cultural anchors. Distractor pool: collective nouns, measurement subjects.
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns plot and character of Little Women / Dickens; here the works are just neutral titles carrying an agreement rule.

name: There is / there are: agreement with the noun after
scope: The there-construction agreement rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION heard everywhere in casual speech -- 'There's many reasons to be careful' sounds normal but is technically wrong; the correct form is 'There ARE many reasons to be careful'. In a THERE-construction, the verb agrees with the noun AFTER it (the real subject), not with THERE. T2: 'There IS a cookie on the plate' (cookie, singular) vs 'There ARE cookies on the plate' (cookies, plural) -- the true subject appears after the verb. T3: name the pattern -- this is called an EXPLETIVE CONSTRUCTION or DUMMY-SUBJECT construction; THERE fills the subject slot syntactically but the real subject follows. T4: the trap with a compound noun after -- 'There ARE a cookie and a glass of milk on the tray' (compound subject, plural verb) sounds clunky, so writers often rewrite ('A cookie and a glass of milk ARE on the tray'). But 'There IS a cookie and a glass of milk' is also heard and accepted informally. T5: the identify-and-fix task -- given a passage, spot every THERE-construction where the verb doesn't agree with the following noun and rewrite each.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.143 (there-constructions); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'there is, there are'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Expletive (linguistics)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the dummy-subject concept.
framing_note: Punchline via the ubiquitous casual 'there's' with plural nouns -- the kid hears it every day and now knows it's wrong. Apolitical examples (cookies, reasons, students, cars). Vocab-teaching at T3 defines EXPLETIVE CONSTRUCTION inline. Distractor pool: subject-verb basics, compound subjects.

name: Data, media, agenda: Latin plurals meeting modern usage
scope: The evolving-usage cases. T1: the classic contested sentence -- 'The data IS clear' (heard everywhere) vs 'The data ARE clear' (scientific-journal style). Both are used; which is right depends on register. T2: the Latin history -- DATA is originally the Latin plural of DATUM ('a given thing'); MEDIA is the plural of MEDIUM; AGENDA is the plural of AGENDUM. Traditional prescriptive rule: treat them as plural. T3: modern usage -- most speakers now treat these as mass nouns (like 'water' or 'information') and use singular verbs: 'The media IS focused on the story', 'The agenda IS on the table'. Style guides split: AP allows singular, Chicago accepts both, most science journals still require plural. T4: the register choice -- in a lab report or a formal paper, write 'the data ARE'; in a newspaper article or casual writing, 'the data IS' is fine. Both are grammatically defensible; pick the register that fits the audience. T5: the parallel case of AGENDA -- 'The agenda IS long' is universal in modern usage (nobody writes 'the agenda ARE long' anymore); AGENDA has completed the shift to singular. DATA is mid-shift. MEDIA is mostly singular in general use but often plural in academic writing.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entries 'data' and 'media'; Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.14 (foreign plurals); AP Stylebook 2020 entry on 'data'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Data (word)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Latin origin and the singular-vs-plural usage split across style guides.
framing_note: Prescriptive-vs-descriptive borderline call -- vision_mandated TRUE because this is exactly the register-aware stance the bank framing calls out. Teach BOTH forms; don't collapse to one. Distractor pool: other Latin plurals (criteria vs criterion), collective nouns, indefinite pronouns.

name: None: singular or plural depending on referent
scope: The most misunderstood indefinite pronoun. T1: the zombie-rule wrong-version -- 'NONE means NOT ONE, so it must be singular' -- this is a 19th-century myth that has NEVER matched actual usage; NONE has been used with plural verbs since Old English. T2: the two correct forms -- 'None of the cookies IS left' (treating none as 'not one') and 'None of the cookies ARE left' (treating none as 'none of them, they are gone') -- both are grammatically correct, and both have been used by careful writers for centuries. T3: the sense-guides-the-verb rule -- if you MEAN 'not one' emphatically ('None of the answers IS correct -- every single one is wrong'), go singular; if you mean 'none of them collectively' ('None of the students WERE ready for the test'), go plural. Merriam-Webster and Chicago both explicitly say the plural is MORE COMMON in modern usage. T4: the mass-noun case -- 'None of the water IS drinkable' (water is uncountable, singular verb is required); the plural is only an option when the object is a count noun. T5: identify the zombie -- given a style handbook that insists 'NONE is always singular', explain that this is a prescriptive myth invented in the 1800s and not supported by actual English usage, historical or modern.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'none' (explicitly rejects the 'always singular' rule); Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.70. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'None (word)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Old English usage history and the 19th-century prescriptive myth.
framing_note: Zombie-rule debunking; vision_mandated TRUE (prescriptive-vs-descriptive contested call per bank framing). Punchline via the surprise that a rule most kids have been taught turns out to be a myth. Apolitical examples (cookies, students, water). Distractor pool: other indefinite pronouns, subject-verb basics.

name: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: matching number and person
scope: The parallel rule to subject-verb, but for pronouns. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'A student should bring THEIR book' -- some old style guides call this wrong (see the singular-they topic for the debunking); but everyone agrees that 'A student should bring OUR book' is wrong because OUR doesn't match A STUDENT in number. T2: define ANTECEDENT in-context -- the noun a pronoun refers back to. In 'Maria found her keys', HER is the pronoun and MARIA is the antecedent. In 'The dogs chased their tails', THEIR refers back to the dogs. T3: the standard cases -- singular antecedent takes singular pronoun ('The girl brought her lunch'); plural antecedent takes plural pronoun ('The girls brought their lunches'). Number and person must match. T4: the ambiguity trap -- 'When Sarah spoke to her mother, she was upset' -- WHO was upset, Sarah or her mother? An ambiguous antecedent is a real error; rewrite ('When Sarah spoke to her mother, Sarah was upset' or 'her mother was upset'). T5: the collective-noun echo -- 'The team celebrated ITS victory' (American, treating team as one unit) vs 'The team celebrated THEIR victory' (also common, treating members individually). Whichever you pick, be CONSISTENT within a sentence -- 'The team is celebrating their victory' mixes singular verb with plural pronoun and jars.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.30 (pronoun-antecedent agreement); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'agreement: pronoun and antecedent'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Pronoun' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the antecedent definition and the number/person matching rules.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines ANTECEDENT inline. Punchline via clear ambiguity error at T4 (WHO was upset?). Apolitical examples (school, family, sports). Distractor pool: singular-they cases, reflexive pronoun errors, subject-verb agreement.

name: Singular they: used since Chaucer, banned in the 1800s, back now
scope: The zombie-superstition debunking. T1: the canonical CONTESTED sentence -- 'Each student took THEIR seat'. Some 20th-century handbooks called this wrong. Actual English usage since Chaucer has always allowed it. T2: the history -- singular THEY appears in Chaucer's 'The Pardoner's Prologue' (c. 1390), in Shakespeare (Comedy of Errors, Hamlet), in Jane Austen (Pride and Prejudice, 1813 -- 'every body began to feel THEIR own consequence'). It is NOT a modern invention; it is older than Modern English. T3: the 19th-century invention -- the 'singular THEY is wrong' rule was invented by prescriptive grammarians in the 1700s and 1800s who wanted English to imitate Latin. Anne Fisher's 1745 grammar was among the first to insist 'he' should be used for a person of unknown sex; this became the schoolroom standard for two centuries and is now widely rejected. T4: modern style guides -- the AP Stylebook (2017), Chicago Manual of Style (17th edition, 2017), and Merriam-Webster (2019, Word of the Year) all explicitly accept singular THEY. Only the most rigid prescriptive texts still forbid it. T5: the practical judgment -- 'A student should bring their book' is now standard; 'A student should bring his or her book' is grammatically correct but wordy; 'A student should bring his book' is archaic and often reads as excluding half the class. Pick THEIR unless a rigid style guide requires otherwise.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'they, their, them'; Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.48 (singular they); Oxford English Dictionary entry 'they' with historical citations. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Singular they' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Chaucer/Shakespeare/Austen citation history and the 1745 Anne Fisher origin of the prohibition.
framing_note: Vision_mandated TRUE -- the bank's framing explicitly stances against the zombie prohibition. Punchline via the surprise that Shakespeare and Austen used the construction the schoolteacher marks wrong. Historical accuracy rail: verify the Chaucer, Shakespeare, and Austen citations before writing rungs. Apolitical framing -- this is a HISTORY-OF-ENGLISH point, not an identity-politics point; keep it linguistic.

name: Reflexive pronouns: myself is not a fancy 'me' or 'I'
scope: The reflexive-vs-personal-pronoun distinction. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION heard in every business email -- 'Please contact John or MYSELF with any questions' -- MYSELF is wrong here; the correct form is 'Please contact John or ME'. Speakers use MYSELF because they think it sounds more formal or polite; it doesn't, it sounds ungrammatical to careful ears. T2: define REFLEXIVE PRONOUN in-context -- a pronoun ending in -SELF or -SELVES that refers back to the SUBJECT of the same clause. 'I hurt MYSELF' (subject I, object myself); 'She taught HERSELF Spanish' (subject she, object herself). The reflexive requires the subject to be the same person. T3: the two correct uses of MYSELF -- (1) REFLEXIVE: 'I cut myself shaving' (I is the subject, myself is the object, same person); (2) EMPHATIC/INTENSIVE: 'I myself made the cake' (myself emphasizes I, doesn't replace it). Any other use is wrong. T4: fix the sentence -- 'The report was written by John and myself' should be 'The report was written by John and ME' (object of the preposition BY, no reflexive). 'John and myself went to the meeting' should be 'John and I went' (subject, needs I). T5: the test -- drop the other person and read the sentence with just the pronoun: 'Please contact myself' (obviously wrong -- so use ME); 'Myself went to the meeting' (obviously wrong -- so use I). If MYSELF sounds wrong alone, it's wrong in the pair.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.51-5.52 (reflexive and intensive pronouns); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'myself'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Reflexive pronoun' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the two-legitimate-uses framing and the emphatic-vs-reflexive distinction.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines REFLEXIVE PRONOUN inline with example. Punchline via the everywhere-you-hear-it business-email misuse ('please contact myself'). Apolitical examples (work, meetings, cake, shaving). Distractor pool: I-vs-me case errors, who-vs-whom, pronoun-antecedent errors.

name: Who vs whom: the he/him substitution trick
scope: The paradigm case of pronoun case, with the easiest possible trick. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'WHOM shall I say is calling?' sounds fancy but is wrong -- WHO is the subject of IS CALLING. Correct: 'WHO shall I say is calling?'. T2: define the WHO/WHOM distinction in-context -- WHO is the SUBJECT form (does the action); WHOM is the OBJECT form (receives the action). Same difference as HE/HIM or SHE/HER, just with a Q-word. T3: the substitution trick -- rewrite the sentence with HE or HIM in place of WHO/WHOM. If HE fits, use WHO; if HIM fits, use WHOM. 'WHO/WHOM did you invite?' becomes 'You invited HIM' -- HIM fits, so WHOM is correct: 'WHOM did you invite?'. T4: the tricky embedded-clause case -- 'The man WHO I think won' vs 'The man WHOM I think won' -- test with HE/HIM: 'I think HE won' -- HE fits, so WHO is correct: 'The man WHO I think won'. The 'I think' is a parenthetical and doesn't change the case. T5: the register judgment -- in formal writing (essays, business letters, cover letters), get WHO/WHOM right. In casual speech, WHOM is fading fast and 'Who did you invite?' is universally accepted. Merriam-Webster notes that WHOM survives mostly after prepositions ('to WHOM it may concern', 'for WHOM the bell tolls') and is otherwise disappearing from natural English.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.63-5.64 (who and whom); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'who, whom' (notes the register-decline). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Who (pronoun)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the he/him substitution trick and the register-decline observation.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines subject-vs-object case with the parallel HE/HIM. Punchline via the fancy-sounding-but-wrong 'whom shall I say is calling'. Practical trick at T3 makes the rule USABLE. Register nuance at T5 (light stance -- teach the standard, note the informal). Distractor pool: I-vs-me errors, reflexive pronoun errors.

name: Between you and I: the pronoun-after-preposition trap
scope: The hypercorrection error the whole country makes. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'BETWEEN YOU AND I, I think he's wrong' -- BETWEEN is a preposition, and pronouns after prepositions take the OBJECT case: BETWEEN YOU AND ME. This is the exact opposite of what most speakers say. T2: the drop-the-other-person test -- 'Between I, I think he's wrong' obviously sounds wrong; 'Between me, I think he's wrong' at least sounds like the right pronoun form. In a compound, use the case each pronoun would take alone. T3: define PREPOSITION in-context -- a small word (in, on, at, by, for, with, from, of, between, among) that shows relationship. Pronouns after prepositions are always OBJECTS, so they take object case (me, him, her, us, them, whom). T4: fix the sentence -- 'The gift is for John and I' should be 'for John and me'; 'She sat next to him and I' should be 'next to him and me'; 'It's a secret just between him and I' should be 'between him and me'. In every case, drop the other name and the correct pronoun is obvious. T5: the origin of the mistake -- kids get scolded for 'Me and John went to the store' (should be 'John and I went'), so they OVERCORRECT and start using I everywhere, even where ME is correct. Both errors -- 'me went' and 'between you and I' -- come from not knowing the case rule; learn the rule and both go away.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.44 (pronoun case after prepositions); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'between you and I' (documents the hypercorrection). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hypercorrection' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the schoolroom-overcorrection origin of the error.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T3 defines PREPOSITION with a list. Punchline via the ubiquity of the error (kid will hear 'between you and I' every week from adults). Drop-the-other-name test at T2 gives the kid a usable check. Apolitical examples (gifts, seating, secrets). Distractor pool: reflexive pronoun errors, subject-verb agreement.

name: I vs me in compound subjects and objects
scope: The everyday pronoun-case mistake in compound noun phrases. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION heard on every playground -- 'ME AND MY BROTHER went to the park' -- ME is wrong; the correct form is 'MY BROTHER AND I went to the park' (I is the subject of WENT). Also polite convention puts the other person first. T2: the drop-the-other-person test -- 'Me went to the park' obviously sounds wrong; 'I went to the park' is correct; therefore 'My brother and I went'. Use the case each pronoun would take alone. T3: the mirror error -- 'The teacher gave the book to JOHN AND I' -- I is wrong; TO takes object case: 'The teacher gave the book to JOHN AND ME'. Drop the other name: 'gave the book to I' sounds wrong; 'gave the book to me' is correct. T4: fix each sentence -- 'She invited John and I to dinner' -> 'John and me' (object of invited); 'John and me went to the store' -> 'John and I' (subject); 'The prize was shared by her and I' -> 'her and me' (object of preposition by). T5: the polite-order convention -- in English, when you list yourself with others, YOU GO LAST: 'My brother and I' (not 'I and my brother'); 'Sarah and me' (not 'Me and Sarah'). This is a courtesy convention, not a grammar rule -- both orders are grammatical, but the you-last order is standard in polite writing.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.43-5.44 (pronoun case in compounds); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'I' (documents both errors). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'English personal pronouns' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the case rules and the you-last politeness convention.
framing_note: Punchline via the WRONG version being what everyone actually says on the playground. Drop-the-other-name trick at T2 gives the usable check. Apolitical examples (park, park, dinner, prize). Distractor pool: between-you-and-I errors, reflexive misuse, who-vs-whom.

name: Each and every: always singular, no matter what follows
scope: The distributive-pronoun singular rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'EACH of the students HAVE a book' sounds natural but is wrong; correct is 'EACH of the students HAS a book'. EACH is always singular, regardless of the plural noun following it. T2: EVERY works the same way -- 'EVERY boy and girl WAS at the party' (not WERE); EVERY makes even a compound subject singular. T3: define DISTRIBUTIVE PRONOUN in-context -- a word that picks out individual members of a group one at a time (each, every, either, neither). Because it picks out ONE at a time, the verb is singular. T4: the intervening-plural trap -- 'Each of the boys IS ready' (not ARE); 'Every one of the answers IS wrong' (not ARE); the prepositional phrase between EACH/EVERY and the verb never changes the singular pronoun. T5: EACH as a postpositive modifier -- when EACH follows a plural subject, the verb goes with the plural subject: 'The students each HAVE a book' (subject STUDENTS, plural verb HAVE, with EACH as a distributive modifier). Same idea, different word order, different verb form -- because the actual subject changes.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.69 (distributive pronouns); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'each'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Distributive pronoun' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the always-singular rule and the postpositive-EACH case.
framing_note: Punchline via the natural mis-hearing ('each of the students HAVE' feels right). Vocab-teaching at T3 defines DISTRIBUTIVE PRONOUN inline. Apolitical examples (students, books, boys, girls, answers). Distractor pool: indefinite pronouns (everyone), compound subjects, collective nouns.

name: Either and neither: singular as subjects, agreement with correlatives
scope: The either/neither agreement rules across two constructions. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'EITHER of the answers ARE correct' sounds okay but is wrong; correct is 'EITHER of the answers IS correct'. As a subject alone, EITHER is singular. T2: NEITHER works the same way -- 'NEITHER of the twins WAS home' (not WERE); NEITHER as a subject is singular. T3: the correlative-pair rule -- when EITHER...OR or NEITHER...NOR joins subjects, the verb agrees with the NEARER subject (see the compound-with-or/nor topic): 'Either the cat or the dogs ARE outside' (dogs, plural, nearer); 'Neither the dogs nor the cat IS outside' (cat, singular, nearer). T4: the mixed-person case -- 'Neither he nor I AM going' -- agreement is with I (person AND number of the nearer subject); 'Neither I nor he IS going' -- agreement is with he. Most writers rewrite these to avoid the awkwardness ('He isn't going, and neither am I'). T5: the practical writer's rule -- if a correlative-subject sentence sounds wrong either way, REORDER the subjects so the plural or the natural-sounding subject is closer to the verb. Grammar and ear both improve.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.69, 5.141 (either, neither, either...or, neither...nor); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entries 'either' and 'neither'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Correlative conjunction' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the pair-with-nearer-subject rule and the mixed-person case.
framing_note: Punchline via the mismatch between everyday speech and the standard rule. Apolitical examples (answers, twins, pets, homework). Overlaps intentionally with the OR/NOR topic on the correlative case (this topic focuses on EITHER/NEITHER as subjects; the OR/NOR topic focuses on the nearer-subject rule). Distractor pool: each-and-every, indefinite pronouns.

name: Relative clauses: verb agrees with the noun WHO/THAT refers to
scope: The tricky agreement in relative clauses. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'She is one of those people who LIKES to be early' sounds okay but is wrong; correct is 'She is one of those people who LIKE to be early'. WHO refers to PEOPLE (plural), so the verb inside the WHO-clause is plural. T2: define RELATIVE CLAUSE in-context -- a clause starting with WHO, WHICH, or THAT that describes a noun. In 'the students who study', 'who study' is a relative clause modifying STUDENTS. The verb in the clause agrees with the noun the WHO/WHICH/THAT points back to. T3: 'The book THAT is on the table' (book, singular, verb is IS); 'The books THAT are on the table' (books, plural, verb is ARE). Track the noun the relative pronoun modifies -- that's your subject for the clause's verb. T4: the ONE OF THOSE trap in depth -- 'He is one of those runners who always FINISHES first' vs 'He is one of those runners who always FINISH first'. Standard rule: the WHO refers to RUNNERS (plural), so plural verb FINISH. But if the writer means to single HIM out, some accept the singular verb; Chicago and Merriam-Webster both recommend the plural in careful writing. T5: the identify-and-fix task -- given a passage with several relative clauses, flag every clause where the verb doesn't agree with the noun the WHO/THAT modifies, and rewrite.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.144 (relative-clause agreement); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'one of those who'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Relative clause' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the antecedent-agreement rule and the 'one of those' controversy.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines RELATIVE CLAUSE inline with example. Punchline via the widespread 'one of those people who likes' error. Apolitical examples (people, books, runners, students). Distractor pool: subject-verb basics, pronoun-antecedent, who-vs-whom.

name: Tense sequence: reported speech shifts backward
scope: The tense-agreement rule in reported speech. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'She said that she IS tired' when reporting past speech sounds off; correct in traditional reported speech is 'She said that she WAS tired' -- the tense inside the quote shifts BACK one step when the reporting verb is past. T2: define REPORTED SPEECH in-context -- turning a direct quote ('I am tired') into an indirect statement ('she said that she was tired'). Direct: 'I am hungry'; Reported: 'He said (that) he was hungry'. Present tense in the quote shifts to past. T3: the full shift table -- Present (am) shifts to Past (was); Past (was) shifts to Past Perfect (had been); Will shifts to Would; Can shifts to Could; May shifts to Might. 'She said, I WILL call you' becomes 'She said she WOULD call me'. T4: the exception for still-true statements -- if the quoted content is a general truth still valid, the present tense can be kept: 'Galileo said that the earth ORBITS the sun' (not ORBITED -- it still does); 'The teacher said that water BOILS at 100 degrees' (still true). Judgment call; both forms are correct. T5: identify and fix -- given a paragraph mixing direct and reported speech, ensure every reporting verb triggers the correct backshift, and flag any still-true statements where the present can be kept.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.128 (sequence of tenses); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'sequence of tenses'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sequence of tenses' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the full backshift table and the still-true exception.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines REPORTED SPEECH inline with example. Punchline via the mid-sentence tense clash ('she said she IS tired' -- doesn't fit). Historical example at T4 (Galileo, water boiling) is factual, apolitical. Distractor pool: subject-verb agreement errors, pronoun errors.

name: Subjunctive mood: 'If I WERE you' vs 'If I WAS you'
scope: The mood agreement rule for hypothetical statements. T1: the canonical PAIR -- 'If I WAS you, I would apologize' (heard everywhere in casual speech) vs 'If I WERE you, I would apologize' (the formal standard). Both are grammatical in different registers; the WERE form is the SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD and is required in formal writing. T2: define SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD in-context -- a verb form used for hypothetical, contrary-to-fact, or wished-for statements. English has three moods: INDICATIVE (statements of fact -- 'I am hungry'), IMPERATIVE (commands -- 'Be quiet!'), and SUBJUNCTIVE (hypotheticals -- 'If I were rich'). T3: the trigger phrases for subjunctive -- (a) contrary-to-fact IF clauses ('If I were you', 'If she were here'); (b) WISHES ('I wish I were taller', 'She wishes she were done'); (c) demand/suggest/insist verbs ('The judge demanded that he BE present', not IS present; 'I suggest she TAKE the job', not TAKES). T4: the distinctive form -- English subjunctive mostly differs from indicative in only ONE place: WAS becomes WERE for all persons ('I were', 'he were', 'she were'), and third-person verbs drop the -S ('that he take', not 'that he takes'). Otherwise the forms match. T5: the modern-register call -- in casual speech, 'If I was you' is widely accepted; in formal writing, essays, business letters, use 'If I were you'. The subjunctive is fading from casual English but still expected in formal register. Merriam-Webster explicitly notes both are used.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.125-5.126 (subjunctive mood); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'subjunctive'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'English subjunctive' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the trigger phrases and the register-decline observation.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2 defines the three MOODS inline. Punchline via the widespread 'if I was you' being informally accepted while 'if I were you' is the taught standard. Register-aware framing (light stance -- teach the standard, note the casual). Apolitical examples (apologies, wishes, jobs). Distractor pool: tense errors, subject-verb basics.

name: Number, majority, half: verb depends on what's being counted
scope: The 'depends on what follows' agreement family. T1: the canonical PAIR -- 'A number of students ARE absent' (plural, common) vs 'The number of students IS growing' (singular). The article makes the difference: A NUMBER OF (plural, meaning 'many'); THE NUMBER OF (singular, meaning 'the count'). T2: MAJORITY works the same way -- 'The majority of voters ARE undecided' (plural, treating voters individually); 'A majority of two-thirds IS required' (singular, treating majority as one quantity). Meaning controls the verb. T3: HALF, PART, PERCENT of X -- these depend entirely on X. 'Half of the pie IS gone' (pie is singular/mass); 'Half of the pies ARE gone' (pies are plural/count). 'Fifty percent of the water IS used' vs 'Fifty percent of the students ARE ready'. T4: LOT works the same way in casual usage -- 'A LOT OF students ARE here' (plural); 'A LOT OF work IS involved' (singular, work is mass); 'LOTS OF' follows the same pattern. All depend on the noun after OF. T5: identify the pattern -- given a paragraph with several 'X of Y' subjects, determine each verb by checking whether Y is singular/mass or plural/count, and whether the phrase is a total ('the number' -- singular) or a set of individuals ('a number' -- plural).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.145 (number of, majority of); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entries 'number, a' and 'majority'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Subject-verb agreement' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 'depends on the object of OF' rule across number/majority/half/lot.
framing_note: Punchline via the article-swap flip (A NUMBER vs THE NUMBER, same words, different verb). Apolitical examples (students, pie, water, voters in the abstract -- avoid current political framings). Distractor pool: measurement subjects, collective nouns, indefinite pronouns.
